Then that value is the top of the range. ui=False marks a value that its group shows with its own controls. reset=False keeps a value when you use the defaults of its group: the theme, and the speech engine and model.


source

add
def add(
    name:str, group:str, label:str, help:str, dflt, lo:NoneType=None, hi:NoneType=None, more:bool=False,
    choices:NoneType=None, unit:str='', pct:bool=False, store:str='file', ui:bool=True, reset:bool=True
):
Add the setting name to SETTINGS and return its row.


The Look group keeps its own controls: the theme swatches and the mode. The Learning group holds the three values of your profile.
The Walks group sets the size of a walk and of a side walk.
The Talks group sets how a talk runs: the questions, the time, the vote and the room.
The Checks and grading group sets the tries, the grade of a shaky pass, and when an idea counts as learned.
The Review group sets the time to the next review. A daily limit on review is new: 0 means no limit, as before.
The Links group sets how much of a link the tutor gets. The pages read by default can not be more than the page cap.
The Research group sets the web search for a step with no source. The tutor searches the web for the idea, reads the best pages, and quotes one passage word for word. When research is off, the tutor does no web search, and the step says that the text is in the tutor’s words.
The Speech to text group keeps the engine and the model, and the pauses at which the mic cuts what you say. The Screen guide group has the voice and the look of a point mark. A point mark is weaker than a circle in each look, so a circle is always the main mark of a step. The default is tick, because it has no ring that looks like a circle.
The Speaking voice group picks who reads the steps of the screen guide aloud. pocket runs Pocket TTS on this Mac. openai sends each line to OpenAI. browser is the voice of the browser (or of the Mac in the overlay). The voice module reads these values. The default is pocket. Until its model is downloaded, the browser speaks. A value from before 0.0.16 (kokoro or hf) is not one of the choices, so it reads as pocket. The speed is only for OpenAI: Pocket TTS has no speed.
The Models group has the default model and one model for each task. An empty value uses the default model. The tasks after extract borrow the model of an older task when they have none: BORROWS says which. The screen guide (guide) and its figure labels (guide_vision) use the model for hints until you pick one. The reply caps are in tokens.
The Lists group sets how many items show in the lists of the app. All of it is under “More”.
Each group except Prompts has rows, and each row is in a group. The Prompts group lists the prompts of prompts.PROMPTS.

assert set(GROUPS) - {'prompts'} == {r.group for r in SETTINGS.values()}
assert all(r.kind != 'int' or r.lo <= r.dflt for r in SETTINGS.values())
len(SETTINGS)

title: settings
text:
The file
DFLT_SETTINGS is the default of each section: the rows that the file keeps, the saved prompt texts and the models that the Settings page downloaded. settings() gives the saved settings over the defaults. A section that is not a dict in the file is ignored, and a top-level key that is not known is dropped.


source

cfg_dir
def cfg_dir()->pathlib.Path:
The folder for abhyasa’s settings and keys: $ABHYASA_CONFIG, else ~/.config/abhyasa.


_saved reads the file only when it changed, so a value read in a loop costs one stat.


source

settings
def settings()->dict:
The saved settings over the defaults.


save_settings writes the file: first a temporary file with its own name, then a rename, so a crash never leaves half a file. A lock keeps two changes from the web app apart. It does not keep a value that is the default. update_settings changes keys in one section.


source

update_settings
def update_settings(
    section:str, **kw
)->dict:
Change some keys in one section of the settings.




source

save_settings
def save_settings(
    d:dict
)->dict:
Write all the settings.


With no file, settings() gives the defaults. A change in one section keeps the others.

test_eq(settings()['walks']['steps'], 12)
update_settings('stt', segment=False)
test_eq(settings()['stt']['segment'], False)
test_eq(settings()['look'], dict(theme='paper', mode='auto', keys_float=True))
update_settings('stt', segment=True)

A file from before this table still loads: its sections update the defaults, and the new sections get their defaults.

_path().write_text(json.dumps(dict(stt=dict(engine='mlx', model='m', segment=True), models=dict(question='', grade='', hint='', lesson=''),
                                   tokens=dict(question='', grade='', hint='', lesson='', extract=''), look=dict(theme='ink', mode='dark'), prompts={}, downloaded=[])))
d = settings()
test_eq((d['stt']['engine'], d['stt']['pause'], d['look']['theme'], d['walks']['steps'], d['models']['extract']), ('mlx', 700, 'ink', 12, ''))
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

A file that is not JSON, or a section that is not a dict, gives the defaults. An unknown top-level key is dropped.

_path().write_text('{not json')
test_eq(settings()['walks']['steps'], 12)
_path().write_text(json.dumps(dict(walks=5, mine=1)))
d = settings()
test_eq((d['walks']['steps'], 'mine' in d), (12, False))
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

title: settings
text:
Read one value
fit makes a saved value fit its row. A number outside the range gets the nearest end. A value of the wrong type gets the default. A whole number can come as 12.0 from a form; it stays a whole number. A choice must be one of the choices.


source

fit
def fit(
    r, v
):
The value v made to fit row r: clamped to the range, or the default for the wrong type.




source

top
def top(
    r
):
The top of the range of row r: a number, or the value of the row that r.hi names.


val gives the value of a row now: the saved value made to fit, else the default. The engine calls it each time it needs the value.


source

dflt
def dflt(
    name:str
):




source

val
def val(
    name:str
):
The value of the setting name now.




source

raw
def raw(
    name:str
):
The saved value of name as it is in the file, or None.


sources.roots is a text list, one path for each line. A source folder has the same rules as a folder that you name: it must be in your home folder, it must not be the home folder itself, and no part of it can be hidden or a link. source_root_why gives the reason when a path breaks a rule. roots gives the paths that keep the rules, and dropped_roots gives the others with their reasons, so the Settings page can show them.


source

dropped_roots
def dropped_roots()->list:
The lines of sources.roots that abhyasa does not use, each as (line, reason).




source

roots
def roots()->list:
The paths of the setting sources.roots that keep the rules of source_root_why, one for each line that is not empty.




source

source_root_why
def source_root_why(
    p
)->str:
Why abhyasa does not read the source folder p: outside the home folder, the home folder itself, hidden, or a link. ’’ when it can.



test_eq(roots(), ['~/code/personal/orgs'])

A saved 50 ideas becomes 30, the most. A string gives the default. A share above 1 becomes 1.

update_settings('walks', steps=50, hands='a lot', note=40.0)
test_eq((val('walks.steps'), val('walks.hands'), val('walks.note')), (30, 1/3, 40))
update_settings('walks', hands=1.5, steps=1)
test_eq((val('walks.hands'), val('walks.steps')), (1., 3))
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

The top of the pages read by default is the page cap.

update_settings('links', pages=40, cap=10)
test_eq((val('links.pages'), val('links.cap')), (10, 10))
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

The look of a point mark is one of three choices. A look that is not a choice gives the default, tick.

update_settings('guide', point='dot')
test_eq(val('guide.point'), 'dot')
update_settings('guide', point='arrow')
test_eq((val('guide.point'), SETTINGS['guide.point'].choices), ('tick', ('tick', 'dot', 'ring')))
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

title: settings
text:
Change one value
set_val saves a value made to fit its row, and returns it. reset puts back the default of one row, and reset_group of each row in a group. changed is true when a value is not its default. clamped gives the value in the file when it was outside the range, so the page can say so.


source

clamped
def clamped(
    name:str
):
The number in the file for name when it was outside the range, else None.




source

changed
def changed(
    name:str
)->bool:




source

reset_group
def reset_group(
    group:str
)->list:
Use the default of each row of group that the file keeps and that a group reset can change. Return their names.




source

rows
def rows(
    group:str
)->list:
The rows of group, in table order.




source

reset
def reset(
    name:str
):
Use the default of the setting name again.




source

set_val
def set_val(
    name:str, v
):
Save the value v of the setting name, made to fit its row. Return the value in use.


The source folders drop the root of the disk, the home folder itself and a hidden folder.

set_val('sources.roots', '/\n~\n~/.ssh\n~/code/personal/orgs\n')
test_eq(roots(), ['~/code/personal/orgs'])
test_eq([l for l, _ in dropped_roots()], ['/', '~', '~/.ssh'])
reset('sources.roots')

A value saved out of range is saved as the end of the range. reset and reset_group put back the defaults.

test_eq(set_val('walks.steps', 99), 30)
test_eq(raw('walks.steps'), 30)
assert changed('walks.steps') and not changed('walks.note')
reset('walks.steps')
test_eq(val('walks.steps'), 12)
set_val('checks.tries', 5); set_val('checks.near', 8)
test_eq(sorted(reset_group('checks')), ['checks.near', 'checks.tries'])
test_eq((val('checks.tries'), val('checks.near')), (3, 7))
update_settings('walks', steps=50)
test_eq(clamped('walks.steps'), 50)
# a number typed by hand as text works, and text that is not a number gives the default
update_settings('tokens', hint='900', grade='many')
test_eq((val('tokens.hint'), val('tokens.grade')), (900, 2048))
# a value that the profile keeps has no reset here
test_fail(lambda: reset('learning.pace'), contains='profile')
save_settings(dict(prompts={}, downloaded=[]))

The speaking engine is browser until you change it, and a value that is not an engine gives the default.

test_eq((val('voice.out'), val('voice.out_speed')), ('pocket', 1.))
test_eq(fit(SETTINGS['voice.out'], 'kokoro'), 'pocket')

title: settings
text:
What stays fixed
Some values keep you safe, so they have no setting: the link checks for local addresses, plain HTTP, the link kinds, the HTML allowlist, the check of a pane address, the local-only hosts, the test allowlist, the grade scale and the depth ladder. The room for phones keeps its safety limits fixed too: the bind rule, the join code, the rate limits, the body size and the headers. FIXED names them, and no row may have one of these words in its name.

assert not [n for n in SETTINGS for w in FIXED if w in n]

title: abhyasa
text:
All releases
abhyasa (अभ्यास) is Sanskrit for “steady practice”. It is a tutor for people who want to learn well and keep their minds active. It asks you questions, and it never gives the answer first. You answer by voice or in text, and you can think aloud. The tutor grades your reasoning, not only the result.
abhyasa keeps a learner model for each concept: how deep you know it, how well you recall it now, and when you must review it. It also learns how you learn. If code helps you more than equations, it uses code to teach a weak concept again. Sometimes it uses a different way on purpose, so that you get better at that way too.
The app needs macOS 26 on Apple Silicon. The tutor uses a language model. You choose it from a list in Settings, for example Claude, GPT or a local model. Your answers go to that model. Speech to text runs on your Mac by default. All other data stays in your vault on your Mac.

title: abhyasa
text:
Download
Click the Download for macOS button at the top. Then do these steps:

Unzip Abhyasa.zip.
Move Abhyasa.app to Applications.
Open Abhyasa.
Wait for the first start. The app uses uv to get Python and the abhyasa package one time. This step takes some minutes.

The app needs uv. If you do not have uv, install it with brew install uv. Each release has a Developer ID signature. Apple notarized each release.

Homebrew
brew install --cask vedicreader/tap/abhyasa
The cask also installs uv. To get a new version, run brew upgrade --cask abhyasa. To remove the app, its settings and its Python environment, run brew uninstall --zap --cask abhyasa. The zap does not remove your vault, because other tools use it too.

title: abhyasa
text:
How it works
Each question goes through the same six steps:

Pick. The code chooses the next concept and the depth. A due review comes first. Then a new concept comes, if you know its prerequisites. The app shows the reason.
Ask. A model writes one question at that depth, in one way to learn, such as code or an analogy. It also writes a correct answer and a rubric. You do not see them.
Struggle. You answer. If your answer is wrong, the tutor shows your first error. It gives a small hint, but not the fix. You can ask for hints, one at a time.
Grade. The model grades your answer and your think-aloud. The code grades choice questions. Code that you write runs in Leela.
Update. The result and your confidence change the floor, the ceiling and the next review date of the concept.
Teach. After a miss, the tutor teaches the smallest step that fixes your first error. Then it asks a check question.

When you say “I don’t know X”, X becomes a concept, and it comes first the next time. Progress, under You, shows your strong concepts and your weak spots with their reasons, and “Practice my weak spots” starts a session on them. A closed part shows the ways that you learn best.







term
meaning




concept
one idea that the tutor can ask you about


depth
0 unseen, 1 recognise, 2 recall, 3 explain, 4 apply, 5 transfer


floor
the highest depth that you pass every time


ceiling
the lowest depth where you failed


attempt
one answer, kept as a document in your vault


session
one sitting of questions. abhyasa saves it after each step, so you can continue it after a restart


walk
a path of steps, one idea for each step. A walk comes from a goal, a topic, a paper, a site, a repo or a text. You can see and change the path


profile
what abhyasa knows about you: your background, your goals, the examples that help you and your pace. You can see and change all of it


way to learn
code, maths, an analogy, a worked example, a picture or plain words. Each result counts for the way that the question used


gap
an idea that you said you do not know. It comes before the concept where you said it, but it does not block that concept


hint
one step on a ladder of six, from the least to the most help


lesson
the smallest step that the tutor teaches after a miss. “Another way” (⌥A) teaches it again in a different way


demo
an interactive figure for one concept. You predict, you lock in, and then you change the inputs

title: abhyasa
section: Learn a paper, a topic or a link as a walk
text:
Learn a paper, a topic or a link as a walk
A walk takes you through one source, one idea at a time. You can make a walk from a paper in your vault, a text that you paste, a topic, or a link. Paste it into the Start box on Home. One line says what abhyasa will do with it. When two readings are likely, the box asks you to pick one.
The tutor reads the source and picks the main ideas. A walk has 12 ideas by default. You can change this number in Settings, under Walks. Before you start, the plan page shows each idea and the kind of check for it. You can change the kind for an idea there.
Each idea is one step. A step shows the passage from the source, word for word. It also shows a short note from the tutor and a figure from the source, if the source has one. Each step has one check:

Short answer. You write the idea in your own words, and the tutor grades it.
Demo. You predict what a demo will do, lock in your prediction, and then change the inputs.
Order. You put the parts of the idea in the right order.
Notebook. For an idea that you learn with code, the step gives a notebook task, and you do it in Leela (see “Open in Leela”). abhyasa runs no code.

The tutor picks the kind that fits the idea and your profile. The step shows the reason. Reading never waits for a check. You can read the passage and press “Skip this idea” at any time. A skipped idea stays unseen in your record. A pass or a miss on a check changes your record, as an answer in a session does.
On a walk step, ⌥S sends your answer. When the check is closed, ⌥S goes to the next idea. ⌥W asks for a hint. In a demo, ⌥V keeps the state of the demo. ⌥F still shows all the keys.

A walk from a link
On Add, choose “A link”. These links work: a web page, a documentation site, a PDF, an arXiv link or id, and a GitHub repository or file. A video link does not work. A link to your own computer or to a local network does not work either.
abhyasa fetches the link only when you press Start. The box reads only the text that you type, and it makes no network call. It reads only the pages in the folder of the link, after any redirect. It reads at most the page cap. The default is 8 pages. You can set the number in the Start box, up to the cap in Settings, under Links. The cap is 20 by default.


A walk to a goal, from your folders and repos
Write a goal in the Start box, such as “I want to fine-tune a diffusion model. Use course22 and fastbook. Also fastai/diffusion-nbs.” The box finds the sources that the goal names and shows them under “Sources for this goal”:

a folder on this Mac, by its name or its path. abhyasa looks for a name only in the source folders (Settings, under Research). The default is ~/code/personal/orgs, two levels down. It never searches the whole disk.
a folder or a repo that is in your vault already;
a public GitHub repo, as owner/name or as a link.

Press × to remove a source, or add one with “Add a folder, a repo or a link”. On a Mac, “Pick folders…” opens the folder chooser. Hold ⌘ to pick more than one folder. You can also drop a PDF, a .md or a .txt file on the box. abhyasa reads nothing before you press Start. Then it files each new folder in your vault and clones each public GitHub repo over HTTPS, then plans the walk. abhyasa reads only .ipynb, .md, .txt and .py files (no .py in a folder with notebooks), at most 400 files and 200 MB, and it never runs their code. It reads only folders in your home folder, that you can read, with no hidden folders and no links. For one hour, the walk page shows “Added course22: 24 notebooks.” with Undo.


Your data
Some folders are not to learn from. They are the data that you plan to run the exercises on, for example a folder of Ramayana episodes for a walk that trains a diffusion model. In the Start box, tick “My data” on the folder. Under “Add a source” on the walk page, choose “My data for the exercises”, or add the folder under “Your data” on the course page. Give it a short note. abhyasa does not file the folder and does not learn from it. The course and its walks keep it, the tutor that writes a notebook step sees its name, its note and its files, and the notebook in Leela runs on it, also a notebook that the tutor wrote before you added the folder. The walk page shows your data under Sources. × removes it.
A path alone, such as ~/code/course22, asks one question: “Walk through it” or “Use it for a goal”.
For a goal, the tutor plans the walk top down from the sources that you named. Each step reads its passage from one of those documents. Steps that build your goal get a notebook check. When the goal names two or more sources, or a source folder has more than 40 documents, an agent reads your sources and the web and finds a passage for each idea. A band on the walk says what it reads now. “Show what it did” opens its log in the side pane, and “Stop” stops it. abhyasa keeps a passage only when it is word for word in its document. The agent has no shell, a time limit (Settings, under Research) and a spend limit.
When no passage is found, the step says why, for example “No page had a good quote.” Press “Find a source” to try again, or “Pick a passage yourself”.


A course to your goal
A goal that you type on Start makes a course. The walk that Start makes is stage 1 of the course. “Course” on the walk opens the course page. It shows your goal, “You are here”, the next idea and the reason for it, the stages, what stands between you and the goal, and the sources of the course.
“Ask me where I start” is the level check. It asks a few short questions about what you know. Answer each one with Yes, A little or No, by a tap or by voice. abhyasa then plans the stages. It skips a stage of basics that you know, and it makes a stage that you know a little short.


Change the walk
Press “Change the walk” on the plan page, or on the rail of a step. Each change saves at once, and the Undo bar says what changed. ⌘Z undoes it. “Earlier versions” lists the changes, and you can go back to one.







key
what it does




W, S
move the focus to the idea above or below


⇧W, ⇧S
move the idea up or down. You can also drag its grip


E
open the idea: its passage, its tutor note, its kind of check and its question


A
add an idea after it: by name, from the concept tree or from a source


P
split the idea into smaller ideas


M
merge the idea with the next idea


X
remove the idea. Undo gives it back


R
ask the tutor to write the note and the question again. A text that you changed at that time stays


⌘Z
undo the last change. In a text box, ⌘Z undoes your typing


⌥S
continue the walk



“Pick another passage” shows only passages that are word for word in the walk documents. The editor also says how many checks are hands-on. A notebook step that builds your goal does not count.

title: abhyasa
text:
Rabbit holes
A passage can use an idea that you do not know yet. The step then shows a “This needs” line with each idea that it needs. An idea that is not learned yet has a “Learn it” button.
You have three choices:

A quick primer. A short text that you read in the side pane.
A short side walk. A small walk on that idea, in the side pane.
Its own session. A normal session on that idea, in a new tab.

Press ⌥B to open the offer. Then press 1, 2 or 3. A primer or a side walk opens in a pane beside the step. The paper stays on the left. On a narrow window, the side walk opens in the same tab, with “Back to the paper” at the top.

⌥B opens the offer for the first idea that you do not know.
⌥Z goes back to the paper and closes the pane. Esc also closes it.
A side walk can open another side walk. The limit is 2 levels, and you can change it in Settings, under Walks. Past the limit, only “Own session” is left.
The check that was open on the paper stays open. The answer that you typed there stays in the box. When the side walk ends, the paper tells you what you learned on the way.

The pane opens only pages of abhyasa. A pane address that points to another site is ignored.

title: abhyasa
text:
The screen guide
When you do not get a part of the page, press Caps+E (⌃⌥⇧⌘E), or press Explain in the top bar. Hold the keys to talk, or tap them to type. Then say what you do not get, for example “I don’t get alpha bar”. When you talk, the words stay in the box: change them if you need to, then push Return to send them.
The tutor answers on the page, as a teacher does at a whiteboard. It circles a term in a formula, points to a label in a figure, moves the demo and speaks one short line for each step. The marks stay in place when you scroll.

A says and draws the step again, S goes back one step, and D goes to the next step. Esc stops the board.
A key that you type in a text box or in an editor stays in that box. The board does not move.
You can ask a follow-up question, such as “say that more simply” or “why?”. The guide sends your last 3 questions on this page with it. “Follows up on: …” shows under the box, with × to start fresh. A new page or 10 minutes with no question clears them.
To show a process, a cycle or a small tree, the guide draws a diagram card at the top right of the window: named boxes with arrows between them, with no crossings. The card never covers the page text. For a formula, the guide gives an example from day-to-day life instead, and marks the formula on the page.
After a check grades your answer, ask “explain the gaps”. The guide names the problem in your answer, explains the idea that fixes it, and shows the path to a right answer. While you have tries left, it stops before the final answer.
On the page of an idea, ask “show me …”. The guide opens a demo of your words in a small card. × or Esc closes it.
A pill says where the answer is from: the tutor, your vault or the web. A quote is word for word, with its link.
When a concept has an explainer video, the board can move the video to the right time and quote it. On a concept page, “Find a video” looks on YouTube, or you can paste a link.
A natural voice reads the steps: Pocket TTS, on this Mac (pip install abhyasa[voice]). Its voice is caro_davy, and Settings, Speaking voice, has 20 other English voices. Download it there one time (225 MB). Until then, the browser speaks. You can also pick OpenAI (hosted, with your key) or the browser. The words light up as the voice says them.

The text that the guide sends to the model goes through ramabana’s guard. The guard always masks secrets. It masks personal data only when the ramabana setting cli.pii is redact or refuse (the default is off).

title: abhyasa
section: Teach a topic to a group
text:
Teach a topic to a group
You can present a walk to a group, as a talk. Each idea of the walk becomes one slide. The passage and the figure, or the demo, show to the room. The tutor note becomes your speaker note. The check of the idea becomes a question for the room.

Make a talk from a walk
On the plan of a walk, or on its path page, press “Present this walk”. The editor shows the slides in the order of the walk. A Questions slide and a recap slide come at the end. Set the minutes of your slot. A change to the talk does not change the walk.
The editor changes each slide in its row, and saves at once. W and S move the focus from slide to slide. ⇧W and ⇧S move a slide up or down, or you drag its grip. E opens the slide: its title, the points that the room sees, your speaker note, the passage, the figure, the beats and the question for the room. D duplicates the slide, X removes it, A adds a slide after it and Q adds a pause. R asks the tutor to rewrite the slide, with the chips Simpler, Add an example and Shorter. The Undo bar says what changed, and ⌘Z undoes it. “Earlier versions” lists the changes.
The beats are chips, one press of D each: the passage, the points, the figure, the demo, the question, or words to light. Drag a chip, or move it with ⇧W and ⇧S. Select words in the passage to light them on the slide.
When the walk changes, press “Make the talk again (keeps your edits)”. A part of a slide that you changed stays. A slide whose idea left the walk goes under “Not in the walk any more”, with “Put back” and “Remove”. “Make a second talk” is under More.
In this version the room answers with hands. Keep “Room phones” at “No phones”.


The two windows
Press Present (⌥S). The presenter window shows the slide now, your notes, the next slide, the question card and a clock. The first key that you press opens the audience window. If the browser blocks it, use the link “Open the audience window” at the top.
To show the audience window on the projector, move it to the projector screen and press F in it. F fills the screen. Another key in the audience window only shows a note: the keys work in the presenter window. A reload of the audience window shows the same slide and beat. If you close the audience window, the presenter window tells you, and gives a link to open it again.
The two windows send messages only to each other, in the same browser. Each run of a talk has a new random key. Thus an audience window from an old run cannot show or change a new run.
The Abhyasa app for Mac cannot open the second window. In the app, the presenter window shows the address of the talk. Open that address in your browser to present.


The keys of a talk
All keys work in the presenter window. They do not work while the focus is in a text box or in the demo.







key
what it does




D, space, → or Page Down
the next beat, then the next slide. With a primer open: its next page. A clicker works too


A, ← or Page Up
back one beat. With a primer open: its page before


G, then a number
go to that slide


Q
ask the room, or close the question


R
show the right answer


1 to 6
while a question is open: the option that most hands chose


E
go into the demo. Esc comes out


X
the laser on or off. Move the pointer over the slide, and a dot shows in the audience window


B
blank the room screen, and back


⌥S
the main button: ask the room, show the answer, close the question. On the last slide it ends the talk


⌥B
open a primer beside the slide


⌥Z
close the primer


Esc
close the open question, the demo focus or the side pane. Esc never ends the talk



In a talk window, ⌥T, ⌥Q, ⌥R, ⌥G, ⌥C, ⌥D, ⌥1 to ⌥3 and / do nothing. Thus a key that you press by mistake does not take you away from the talk.


Ask the room with hands
Press Q. The question and its options show in the audience window. The answer does not show. The people in the room put up their hands. Press the number of the option that most hands chose: 1 for A, 2 for B, and so on. Then press R. The right answer and the answer of most hands are lit. After R, “Talk to your neighbour” lets the room talk in pairs about the answer.
On a slide with a demo, press E to go into the demo and change it. The demo in the audience window follows each change. When you choose an answer at a gate of the demo, the room sees your answer. The room sees if your answer is right only after R. If you press “Try another”, the gate opens again in both windows.


The side pane in a talk
Press ⌥B to see the ideas that the slide needs. Press 1 for a quick primer, or 2 for a short side walk. The primer opens beside the slide in both windows, in large type. It has no check. A long primer shows one page at a time: press D for the next page and A for the page before. While it is open, Q asks the room a question about the primer. ⌥Z closes the pane in both windows. A move to a new slide also closes it. A side walk from a talk does not show in your walks or in Continue.


After the talk
On the last slide, press ⌥S, or press “End the talk” at the top. The audience window says “Thank you”, and the presenter window opens “After the talk”. This page shows:

where the room was unsure: each question, with the answer that most hands chose;
the talk, slide by slide, with the time of each slide and each primer beside it;
“Save the recap as one file”: one HTML file with the slides, the passages, and each question with its right answer and the result of the room. It has no speaker notes and no names. Send it by mail or chat. “Look at it first” opens it in the browser;
a follow-up walk on the ideas where the room was unsure, and the primers that you can put in the talk for the next time.



The room does not change your learning
The answers of the room are counts in the talk. They are not your attempts. Your own pick at a demo gate in a talk is not an attempt either. A talk does not change your record, your Continue or your walks.
Settings has a Talks group. It has the minutes for each question, the time to talk to a neighbour, the share of right answers below which a slide is unsure (70% by default), and how long the laser dot stays.

title: abhyasa
text:
Open in Leela
abhyasa runs no code, and it does not install libraries for you. Code, a library or a command-line tool is better to learn in Leela. Leela has the tool environments, code lookup and an agent tutor.
When you add a link, tick “It is a library or a command-line tool”. This makes a tool walk. A tool walk asks short-answer and order checks here, and its code steps are notebooks in Leela.
A step that needs code has an “Open in Leela” link. The link opens Leela in a new tab, on the same walk and step. abhyasa never calls Leela. It reads the file that a running Leela writes, and it makes a link only to an address on this computer.
If Leela does not run, the step says so, and it links to the install page.
What you do in Leela comes back to the step: your code check, your prediction and your run, with its images. A check that passes in Leela marks the step done, and the step offers “Next idea”. The walk end page shows “What you made”.

title: abhyasa
text:
Settings
Settings has every value that you may want to change. The values are in 12 groups:







group
what it sets




Look
the theme and the mode


Learning
your pace, how many questions a session has, and how often the tutor tries a new way to teach you


Walks
how many ideas a walk has, how much is hands-on, how deep a side walk goes, and the length of a passage and a note


Talks
the minutes for each question, the time to talk to a neighbour, when a slide is unsure, and the laser


Checks and grading
the tries for a check, how close an answer must be to pass, hints, and how sure you must be


Review
when a concept comes back, and a limit for each day


Links
the page cap, the time for a link, and how much text abhyasa keeps


Code runner
the time for each test, the whole run, and the size of a file that code writes


Speech to text
the speech engine, the pause that ends a phrase, and the longest phrase


Models
the model for each tutor task, and the limit of its reply


Lists
how many rows each list shows


Prompts
the text of the tutor prompts



Each number has a range. The page shows the range and the default next to the value, for example 3 to 30 · default 12. A value outside its range is not kept. If your settings file has such a value, abhyasa uses the nearest end of the range and tells you on the page. Where a value is not the default, “Use the default” puts the default back. “Use the defaults for this group” does the same for the whole group. “Find a setting” filters the rows as you type.
Some guards have no setting: the closed process with no network, the check of link addresses, plain HTTP for web pages, the check of a pane address, and the rule that abhyasa answers only this computer. A change to a setting works on the next question or the next walk.

title: abhyasa
text:
Keyboard shortcuts
All keys are for the left hand. ⌥ is the Option key. ⌥T, ⌥Q, ⌥R and ⌥G open the tabs Today, Learn, Library and You. ⌥1 to ⌥3 open a sub-tab. To see all the keys, press ⌥F, or press ? outside a text box.
Caps+E (⌃⌥⇧⌘E) opens the screen guide. On the page Change the walk and in the talk editor, W and S move the focus, ⇧W and ⇧S move a row, E opens it, X removes it, R rewrites it and ⌘Z undoes the last change. On the Concepts page, ⌘Z undoes the last change that you made by hand.
If you use Sanketa, it shows the same keys when abhyasa is in front. abhyasa writes the pack ~/.config/sanketa/packs/abhyasa.toml when it starts. It does not write over a pack that you made.

title: abhyasa
text:
Run from source
Install the package and its dependencies:
uv sync
Start the web app on http://127.0.0.1:5077:
uv run abhyasa
The app answers only requests from this Mac. These variables change the defaults:








variable
what it sets
default




ABHYASA_VAULT
the vault file
your vault: $VISHALAKSHI_VAULT, then ~/.vishalakshi/vault.db


ABHYASA_MODEL
the model id for questions, grades, hints and lessons. Choose the model in Settings.
claude/sonnet (Claude Sonnet)


ABHYASA_STT
the speech-to-text engine: mlx, whisper, openai or mlx:<repo>. It has priority over the Settings page. An old gemma reads as mlx.
the Settings page, then mlx (Qwen3-ASR 0.6B)

title: abhyasa
text:
Other ways to use it
The web app, the terminal and the notebooks use the same tutor and the same data.

The web app
The web app is made from blocks in abhyasa/blocks:



block
what it does




today
Home: continue, the reviews that are due, your courses and walks, Teach (your talks) and the Start box


history
You → Progress: this week, what you learned each week, and each past session with what changed, in a fold. Continue (⌥C) is in the top bar


jobs
the activity chip in the top bar: what runs in the background and what ended, each with a link to its page. One event stream tells a page when a job changes


profile
what abhyasa knows about you: a short first conversation, your edits, and the changes that the tutor makes, each with its reason


strengths
on Progress: your strong concepts, your weak spots and the ways that you learn best


session
one sitting with the tutor: one question at a time, with hints, confidence and “I don’t know”


voice
a microphone for each text box. ⌥D speaks into the box that has the focus, on any page


settings
every value that you may change, in groups: the look, learning, walks, checks, review, links, speech, models, list lengths and the tutor prompts. Each number shows its range and its default. A change works on the next question


concepts
Library → Concepts: the tree of concepts, and one page for each concept with its state and Open it in your walk


graph
the concept graph. You can color it by depth, by how well you know each concept, by subject or by due date


search
one search over the learning shelf and the other shelves of your vault


add
the Start box: read what you paste or drop, then make a walk or find concepts


walk
a walk: one step for each idea, with a passage, a note and a check


detour
rabbit holes: a primer, a side walk or a session for an idea that a step needs, with the side pane


demo
interactive demos from rupaka: on a concept page, under a lesson after a miss, and one page for each demo


keys
the keyboard shortcuts (⌥F)



The top bar has three tabs: Home (⌥T), Library (⌥R) and You (⌥G). ⌥Q goes to the Start box on Home. Library and You have sub-tabs under the page title. ⌥1, ⌥2 and ⌥3 open them. The gear at the right end opens Settings. Each page shows where you are, above its title. Esc goes up one level, and Back and Forward work.


Notebooks
In leela or Jupyter, learn shows a question card.
from abhyasa.nb import learn
learn('reciprocal-rank-fusion')

title: abhyasa
text:
Where the data is
All data is on the learning shelf of your vault. Each concept, attempt and session is one document in the vault. Thus your other tools can search it. The tests use a vault in a temporary folder. They never open your real vault.

title: abhyasa
text:
Speech models and their licences
abhyasa does all speech on your Mac with two packages. The models download on first use, from Hugging Face.



what
package (extra)
model
licence




speech to text
mlx-audio (whisper)
Qwen3-ASR 0.6B, 8 bit (1.0 GB), or Whisper large-v3-turbo
Apache-2.0; Whisper: MIT


the voice of the guide
pocket-tts-mlx (voice)
Pocket TTS by Kyutai (225 MB)
code: MIT; weights: CC-BY-4.0



The Pocket TTS weights are by Kyutai, under the CC-BY-4.0 licence. OpenAI speech is a choice in Settings. It sends your audio or the text off your Mac, and it needs your key.

title: abhyasa
text:
Demos
Some ideas are easier to see than to read. A demo is one interactive figure from rupaka. It asks you to predict first. It hides the result until you lock in (⌘↩︎). Then the controls work, and the last line asks a new question.

The tutor makes a demo after two misses on a concept with the same kind of error. It also makes one for a concept with visual: true in its meta. The model writes the demo as data. rupaka checks it in a headless browser. You do not wait for it.
After a miss on a concept that has a demo, the session shows the demo under the lesson.
“Show me a demo” (⌥E) on a concept page shows the newest demo, or makes one.
abhyasa keeps each prediction as an attempt with kind='demo'. A prediction changes the learner model of the concept, as an answer does. A prediction with a reason counts at depth 3 (explain). A prediction without a reason counts at depth 2 (recall).

abhyasa.demo.import_gallery(learning) keeps the rupaka gallery demos, such as vowel sandhi, for the concepts that match.

title: abhyasa
text:
Example
This example runs offline. temp_learning makes a shelf in a temporary vault, and Fake takes the place of the model.

from abhyasa.store import temp_learning
from abhyasa.llm import Fake
from abhyasa.tutor import Tutor


lr = temp_learning()
lr.put('Ranking', 'Order items by a score.', 'ml')
fake = Fake({'You grade one answer': dict(correct=True, grade=8, first_error='', misconception='', feedback='Yes. Only the order counts.')},
            dflt=dict(question='Why can you compare ranks from two systems, but not their scores?', answer='Ranks share one scale.', rubric=['ranks share one scale']))
t = Tutor(lr, fake, context=False)

Ask the first question. why gives the reason for the choice, and method gives the way to learn that the question uses. A new concept starts at depth 3 (explain).

q = t.next()
assert q.why.startswith('next on the frontier: its prereqs are in place')   # a note on the way to learn can follow
assert q.depth == 3
print(q.question)

Answer with high confidence. A solid pass at depth 3 changes the floor to 3.

r = t.answer(q.id, 'A rank is a position, and positions use the same scale in each list.', confidence=80)
assert r.outcome == 'solid'
assert lr.concept('ranking').floor == 3

title: talk
text:
A presenter can give a walk to a group. The talk is a list of slides. Each slide shows a part of the walk, one beat at a time, and it can have one question for the room. This module is the engine of a talk: the shape of a deck, the checks of that shape, the questions, a talk made from a walk, the store calls, the public deck that the room sees, the run log, and the recap after the talk. It imports no web code, so Leela can use the same shape and checks.
The imports are light: the standard library, the store, the walk paths (journey), the demos, the model calls, the prompts and the settings.

title: talk
text:
What a talk is
A talk is a document on the learning shelf, of kind talk. It points at its walk in src and copies what it shows, so a change to the talk never changes the walk. minutes is the slot of the presenter. phones is the choice “Room phones”. live is the id of the run that is open now, or None.
These names give the shape. A slide has one of SLIDE_KINDS, and a question has one of ASK_KINDS.


source

on_stage
def on_stage(
    t:dict
)->dict:
Talk t with no parked slide: the talk that Present gives.




source

parked
def parked(
    s:dict
)->bool:
True when slide s is parked: its idea left the walk. The room never sees it, and it takes no minutes.

title: talk
text:
Slides and beats
Each press of D shows one beat more. passage, body, figure and demo show a part of the slide. ask opens the question. body is a short list of points that the tutor writes for a slide that has no passage. lit:<text> lights a text in the passage, and lit:#<id> lights a part of the figure or the demo. Leela adds lines:a-b and out for its code slides.
A beat that shows a part needs that part on the slide. This table gives the part for each beat.
A figure is an image id, never a path or a URL: asset:<path in the vault assets>. An id with another scheme, a .. part, a leading /, a backslash, a second : or a control character is refused.
The body of a slide is a list of at most BODY_MOST points. Each point is a short text.
A list of short points is a good body. A text, or too many points, is not.

assert _body_ok([]) and _body_ok(['Scores become weights.'])
assert not any(map(_body_ok, ('Scores.', ['a'] * (BODY_MOST + 1), ['x' * (POINT_MOST + 1)], [1])))

A plain path and a path out of the assets folder are not image ids. A good id is.

assert _image_ok('asset:attention/images/fig2.png')
assert not any(_image_ok(f) for f in ('/Users/k/fig.png', 'asset:../vault.db', 'asset:/etc/x.png', 'ws:a.png', 'asset:a:b.png', 'asset:a\\b.png', 'asset:a\nb.png', None))

text:
Questions for the room
A demo gate with fixed options can be a room question with no model call. ask_from_gate and public_ask are thin wrappers over rupaka.poll.of_gate and rupaka.poll.public, so the rules come from rupaka. The options are a list, or {"from": path} in the state of the spec. The answer is {"is": value}, or a path in the state. A path that is not in the state (it needs derive) gives None, and so do fewer than 2 or more than 6 options. The prompt and the options are written as the drawn gate shows them, so the room reads the same text as the demo on the screen: 2.0 shows as 2, a minus is the sign −, a number has at most 4 digits after the point (or the digits that a {path:2} field gives), and None shows as empty.

A name that reads as a question (it ends with ?, or it starts with Why, How, What, When or Which and has more words) is the question. text:
What the slides say
A walk from a paper or a link gives each slide a passage. A walk from a topic does not: its steps have no passage, and the tutor note of a step comes only when a learner opens the step. So the tutor writes the content of each slide when the talk is made. A slide with no passage gets 2 to 4 points for the room. Each slide with no speaker note gets one: what to say, one question to ask the room, and one common confusion to watch for. A slide with a passage keeps it, and gets only the notes.

title: talk
text:
Make it again
A walk can change after you make a talk from it: you add, remove, skip or move ideas, or change a note or a passage. “Make it again” brings these changes into the same talk, and keeps your edits. It matches a slide to a step by the concept slug, never by its place.

A slide whose idea is still in the walk keeps each part that you changed. A part that you did not change takes the new walk, when the step changed.
A new idea gets a new slide, at its place in the walk.
A slide that you added (a pause, questions, a primer) stays after the slide that it followed.
A slide whose idea left the walk moves, in its order, to the end, in the section “Not in the walk any more”.
An idea whose slide you removed stays out.

Your edits are the parts that changed since the talk was made. Each part of a slide as made has a short hash in marks. A part whose hash is not the same now is yours. (The history of the talk is not used for this: it keeps at most 50 changes, and a change of a passage or of more than one field names no field.) A talk made before 0.0.14 has no marks, so each of its slides stays as it is.
slide_marks gives the hash of each part of a slide, and step_mark the hash of the parts of a walk step that a slide uses.

walk_changes counts the ideas that the walk added, removed and moved since the talk was made, and the ideas whose note, passage or check changed in the walk (by the step hash in marks, for an idea that still has its slide). A skipped idea counts as removed. An idea counts as moved when it is not in the longest run of ideas that keep their order (difflib). An old talk with no made_from, or a talk whose walk is gone, gives all zero.

_groups cuts the slides into the part before the first idea, one group for each idea (its slide, then the slides that follow it), the closing slides (the questions and the recap at the end), and the slides that an earlier “Make it again” moved to the end. A second slide of the same idea (a copy) follows the first. A slide that you put back in the talk (own) follows the slide before it, as a pause does.
_kept gives the slide of an idea that is still in the walk. When the step changed, the slide takes the new slide f, except the parts that you changed. A slide that comes back from “Not in the walk any more” takes the section of its step. A merge that does not pass check_talk keeps the old slide. The new marks keep fm, the hash of the step as the new slide was made from it. So when the walk changed the step again during the model calls, the change still counts in walk_changes. When the slide stays as it is, its marks stay too.
again_slides puts it together: the head, then the walk in its order, then the closing slides, then the slides whose idea left the walk. fresh has a new slide for each idea that needs one (a new idea, or a step that changed). fresh gives (slide, fm) for each idea. New slides get new ids. A parked slide keeps its old section in was, so an idea that comes back into the walk brings back all its slides (a pause, a questions slide), each with its section, in its place.

title: talk
text:
Tests
These tests use the small paper in tests/walk_data.py, the walk of tests/talk_data.py and a fake model.
A talk from the walk: one slide for each idea, then the questions and the recap.

lr = temp_learning(); jid = talk_walk(lr); ask = Fake(TALK_RULES)
t = talk_from_walk(lr, ask, jid)
s1, s2, s3 = t.slides[:3]
assert [s['id'] for s in t.slides] == ['s1', 's2', 's3', 's4', 's5']
assert [s['kind'] for s in t.slides] == ['idea', 'idea', 'idea', 'questions', 'recap']

The first slide has the title, the section, the step and the concept of its idea. It shows the passage, and its question is a choice from the short check.

assert (s1['title'], s1['section'], s1['step'], s1['concept']) == ('Sequential computation', '1 Introduction', 0, 'sequential-computation')
assert s1['show']['passage'].startswith('This inherently sequential nature') and s1['show']['figure'] is None and s1['beats'] == ['passage']
assert s1['ask'] == dict(kind='choice', **CHOICE, src=dict(check='short'))

The second slide shows the figure as an image id, and its notes are the note of the step. The third slide shows the demo, and its question comes from the gate hot.

assert s2['show']['figure'] == 'asset:attention/images/fig2.png' and s2['beats'] == ['passage', 'figure'] and s2['notes'] == 'Softmax makes weights from scores.'
assert s3['show']['demo'] == 'softmax-temperature' and s3['beats'] == ['passage', 'demo']
assert s3['ask'] == dict(kind='choice', q='T goes from 1 to 2. What happens to the share of Paris?',
                         options=['It rises', 'It falls', 'It stays the same'], answer=1, src=dict(demo='softmax-temperature', gate='hot'))

The first slide shows a passage, so it keeps it and gets no points. It had no note, so the tutor writes its speaker notes. The second slide had a passage and a note, so it needs no call.

                                                          options=['Left and down', 'Right and down', 'Straight up', 'It stays'], answer=0)
assert ask_from_gate(g['reciprocal-rank-fusion'], 'win') is None   # the answer needs derive
assert ask_from_gate(g['vowel-sandhi'], 'join') is None            # the options need derive
assert ask_from_gate(g['softmax-temperature'], 'nope') is None

The prompt uses the number format of the demo: 2.0 shows as 2, a minus is −, and a field can give the digits.

spec = dict(state=dict(b=2.0, c=-0.5, k=1/3, xs=[1.0, 2.5], on=True, opts=['up', 'down']),
            blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='b is {b}, c is {c}, k is {k} or {k:2}, xs {xs}, {on}, {gone}.', options={'from': 'opts'}, answer={'is': 'up'})])
assert ask_from_gate(spec, 'g')['q'] == 'b is 2, c is −0.5, k is 0.3333 or 0.33, xs 1, 2.5, true, {gone}.'
spec = dict(state=dict(a=[7.25], x=2.5, y=1e-9, n=10, i=float('-inf'), z=None, opts=['p', 'q']),
            blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='{a.0}:{x:0} {y} {n} {i} [{z}]', options={'from': 'opts'}, answer={'is': 'p'})])
assert ask_from_gate(spec, 'g')['q'] == '7.25:3 0 10 −Infinity []'

The options also have the format of the drawn gate, so they are text. The index of the answer comes from the values in the state.

spec = dict(state=dict(opts=[2.0, -1.5, 1/3, None], best=1/3), blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='Which?', options={'from': 'opts'}, answer='best')])
assert ask_from_gate(spec, 'g') == dict(kind='choice', q='Which?', options=['2', '−1.5', '0.3333', ''], answer=2)

Options and an answer from a state path give a choice, and the prompt gets the values of the state. A {name} with no value stays.

spec = dict(state=dict(k=60, opts=['x', 'y'], best='y'), blocks=[dict(type='row', blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='With k = {k} and {m}?',
                                                                                         options={'from': 'opts'}, answer='best')])])
assert ask_from_gate(spec, 'g') == dict(kind='choice', q='With k = 60 and {m}?', options=['x', 'y'], answer=1)

The public part of a question has no answer and no source.

assert public_ask(s3['ask']) == dict(kind='choice', q='T goes from 1 to 2. What happens to the share of Paris?', options=['It rises', 'It falls', 'It stays the same'])
assert public_ask(None) is None

TALK_CASES: each talk gives exactly its problems, and put_talk refuses a talk with a problem.

GOOD = dict(id='t-1', kind='talk', schema=1, title='T', src={'walk': 'w-1'}, minutes=10, phones=False, live=None,
            slides=[dict(id='s1', kind='idea', title='A', section='', notes='', mins=3,
                         show=dict(passage='Scores become weights.', figure='asset:a/fig.png', demo=None),
                         beats=['passage', 'lit:weights', 'figure'], ask=dict(kind='choice', q='Q?', options=['a', 'b'], answer=1))])
for case, want in TALK_CASES: assert check_talk(case) == want, (case, want)
wants = [w for _, w in TALK_CASES]
assert [] in wants and ['schema 2 is not 1'] in wants and ["s1: unknown kind 'video'"] in wants
assert ['s1: the answer 2 is not an option'] in wants and ['s1: a choice needs 2 to 6 options'] in wants
assert ["s1: the beat 'demo' needs a demo to show"] in wants and ["s1: the beat 'lit:gradients' lights text that is not in the passage"] in wants
assert ["s1: the figure '/Users/k/fig.png' is not an image id"] in wants and ["s1: the figure 'asset:../vault.db' is not an image id"] in wants
assert ['s1: the slide id is used twice'] in wants and ["s1: unknown ask kind 'poll'"] in wants and ["s1: unknown beat 'fly'"] in wants
assert ['s1: the answer [0, 0, 1] is not an order of the options'] in wants
test_fail(lambda: lr.put_talk(dict(GOOD, schema=2)), contains='schema 2 is not 1')

clean_slide strips the marks from each field that a person writes, keeps line ends, and never touches the passage.

bad = _case(title='A\u202eB', notes='One.\nTwo\x07', ask=_with_ask(q='Q\u2066?'), show=_with_show(body=['P\ufeff'], passage='Keep\x0c this.'))['slides'][0]
ok = clean_slide(bad)
assert (ok['title'], ok['notes'], ok['ask']['q'], ok['show']['body']) == ('AB', 'One.\nTwo', 'Q?', ['P']) and ok['show']['passage'] == 'Keep\x0c this.'
assert not _ctrl_problems('s1', ok) and bad['title'] == 'A\u202eB'   # a copy: the slide that it gets stays

The good talk of the cases is the same as GOOD.

assert TALK_CASES[0][0] == GOOD



The public deck, the run log and the recap
A talk from the walk, with the figure file in the assets folder.

lr = temp_learning(); jid = talk_walk(lr); t = talk_from_walk(lr, Fake(TALK_RULES), jid)
pub, h = public_deck(t, asset_resolver(lr)), hashlib.sha256(PNG).hexdigest()

A talk made before 0.0.13 kept no source for a passage from a document. When it loads, each such slide gets the source of its walk step. With no walk, the slide says your source, with the title of the talk.

old = deepcopy(t)
for s in old['slides']: s['show'].pop('src', None)
lr.put_talk(old)
test_eq(slide_source(lr.talk(t.id).slides[0]), slide_source(t.slides[0]))
gone = {**deepcopy(old), 'id': 't-gone', 'src': {'walk': 'no-such-walk'}}; lr.put_talk(gone)
g = slide_source(lr.talk('t-gone').slides[0])
test_eq((g.label, g.title, g.href), ('your source', t.title, ''))
lr.drop_talk('t-gone'); lr.put_talk(t);

Each public slide has only the allowed fields. The figure comes by its hash, and the question has no answer.

assert all(set(s) == {'id', 'kind', 'title', 'section', 'passage', 'body', 'figure', 'ask', 'src'} for s in pub.slides)
assert pub.slides[1]['figure'] == h and pub.images == {h: (PNG, 'image/png')}
assert pub.slides[2]['ask'] == dict(kind='choice', q='T goes from 1 to 2. What happens to the share of Paris?', options=['It rises', 'It falls', 'It stays the same'])

The slides as JSON have no notes, no answer, no demo and no path.

js = json.dumps(pub.slides)
assert 'Softmax makes weights' not in js and '"answer"' not in js and 'softmax-temperature' not in js and '/Users/' not in js and '/tmp/' not in js

A slide with beats but no passage beat shows no passage to the room.

t3 = deepcopy(t); t3.slides[0]['beats'] = []
assert public_deck(t3, asset_resolver(lr)).slides[0]['passage'].startswith('This inherently sequential nature')
t3.slides[1]['beats'] = ['figure']
assert public_deck(t3, asset_resolver(lr)).slides[1]['passage'] == ''

A path out of the assets, or a file that is not an image, gives no figure.

t2 = deepcopy(t); t2.slides[1]['show']['figure'] = 'asset:../vault.db'
assert public_deck(t2, asset_resolver(lr)).slides[1]['figure'] is None
(lr.vault.assets('attention')/'images'/'fake.png').write_bytes(b'<script>alert(1)</script>')
t2.slides[1]['show']['figure'] = 'asset:attention/images/fake.png'
assert public_deck(t2, asset_resolver(lr)).images == {}

A figure larger than talks.image_mb does not go to the room, and a resolver that raises gives no figure.

big = lr.vault.assets('attention')/'images'/'big.png'
big.write_bytes(PNG + bytes(val('talks.image_mb') * 2**20))
t2.slides[1]['show']['figure'] = 'asset:attention/images/big.png'
assert public_deck(t2, asset_resolver(lr)).slides[1]['figure'] is None
def boom(f): raise OSError('no disk')
assert public_deck(t, boom).images == {}

The run log keeps the time on each slide. A move on the same slide adds no entry, and the time goes to the last slide.

r = new_run(t, now=100.)
assert r['id'].startswith('run-') and len(r['key']) == 16 and r['at'] == dict(slide='s1', beat=1, blank=False, pane=None, ask=None)
log_go(r, 's2', 1, now=160.); log_go(r, 's2', 2, now=170.); log_go(r, 's3', 1, now=400.)
assert r['shown'] == [dict(slide='s1', at=100., secs=60.), dict(slide='s2', at=160., secs=240.), dict(slide='s3', at=400., secs=0.)]
assert r['at']['slide'] == 's3' and r['at']['beat'] == 1

The hands, the rounds, the side pane and the questions. A question has at most two rounds.

log_main(r, 's1', 'choice', 1)
log_round(r, 's2', 'choice', [20, 2, 1, 1], 24); log_round(r, 's2', 'choice', [22, 1, 1, 0], 24)
test_fail(lambda: log_round(r, 's2', 'choice', [1, 1, 1, 1], 4), contains='at most two rounds')
log_round(r, 's3', 'choice', [11, 10, 4], 25)
log_beside(r, 'softmax', 's3', at=420., secs=120.)
q = log_question(r, 'Is √dk the best number?', at=430., shown=True, note='It keeps the variance near 1.')

log_main also keeps a list, as a copy, for a board or a timeline. A single value stays a single value.

rb, cards = new_run(t, now=0.), (2, 0, 1)
log_main(rb, 's4', 'order', cards); log_main(rb, 's1', 'choice', 1)
assert rb['asks']['s4']['main'] == [2, 0, 1] and rb['asks']['s1']['main'] == 1

end_run closes the last slide. The run is saved, and runs finds it.

end_run(r, now=1300.); lr.put_run(r)
assert q['id'] == 'q1' and r['ended'] == 1300. and r['shown'][-1]['secs'] == 900. and lr.runs(t.id)[0]['id'] == r['id']
assert lr.run(r['id']).asks == r['asks'] and lr.run('run-none') is None

A second save replaces the run, and runs gives the newest run first.

r2 = new_run(t, now=2000.); lr.put_run(r2); r2['people'] = 12; lr.put_run(r2)
assert [x['id'] for x in lr.runs(t.id)] == [r2['id'], r['id']] and lr.run(r2['id']).people == 12 and lr.runs('other') == []

Weak ideas: the last round below 0.7, or hands that chose a wrong option.

w = weak(t, r)
assert [x['slide'] for x in w] == ['s1', 's3']
assert w[1] == dict(slide='s3', title='Scaling by the root of dk', share=.4, top_wrong='It rises', n=25, main=None)
assert (w[0]['share'], w[0]['main'], w[0]['top_wrong']) == (None, 1, 'The largest score only')

A bool is not a hand count: main=True does not make a weak idea.

assert weak(t, dict(asks={'s1': dict(main=True)})) == []

A run question is “What does this print?” It has a question and 2 to 6 options, or none for free words. It has no answer before the run. public_ask keeps its kind, its question and its options.

assert _ask_problems('s1', dict(kind='run', q='What does it print?')) == []                                   # free words, no answer
assert _ask_problems('s1', dict(kind='run', q='What does it print?', options=['1', '2'])) == []
assert _ask_problems('s1', dict(kind='run', q='?', options=['only one'])) != [] and _ask_problems('s1', dict(kind='run', q='?', options=[1, 2])) != []
assert _ask_problems('s1', dict(kind='run', q='?', answer=0, options=['1', '2'])) != []                       # an answer before the run is refused
assert 'run' in ASK_KINDS and ASK_KINDS[:4] == ('choice', 'order', 'words', 'scale')                          # the other kinds stay
assert public_ask(dict(kind='run', q='What does it print?', options=['1', '2'], source='x')) == dict(kind='run', q='What does it print?', options=['1', '2'])

log_output keeps the output of the run for a slide: plain text, at most 2000 characters. The recap shows it as the answer, escaped. weak treats a run question as a choice when an option equals the output and the room’s main pick is known; with no matching option it skips the question.

tr, rr = deepcopy(t), new_run(t, now=0.)
for s in tr['slides']:
    if s['id'] == 's1': s['ask'] = dict(kind='run', q='What does it print?', options=['1', '2', '3'])
log_output(rr, 's1', '<b>2</b>\x00\x07\n' + 'x' * 3000)
assert rr['asks']['s1']['kind'] == 'run' and len(rr['asks']['s1']['output']) == 2000 and '\x00' not in rr['asks']['s1']['output']
rr['asks']['s1']['output'] = '<b>2</b>'
assert recap(tr, rr).slides[0]['output'] == '<b>2</b>'
page = recap_html(tr, rr, asset_resolver(lr))
assert '<pre><b>2</b></pre>' in page and '<b>2</b>' not in page                                      # shown as the answer, escaped
rr['asks']['s1']['output'] = '2'; log_main(rr, 's1', 'run', 0)
assert [w['slide'] for w in weak(tr, rr)][:1] == ['s1'] and weak(tr, rr)[0]['top_wrong'] == '1'                # the room chose 1, the output is 2
log_main(rr, 's1', 'run', 1); assert 's1' not in [w['slide'] for w in weak(tr, rr)]                           # the room chose the output
rr['asks']['s1']['output'] = 'no option has this'; log_main(rr, 's1', 'run', 0)
assert 's1' not in [w['slide'] for w in weak(tr, rr)]                                                        # no option equals the output: skipped

A split vote is from 0.3 to 0.7. A round with no answers is not split.

assert is_split(t.slides[2]['ask'], dict(counts=[11, 10, 4], n=25)) and not is_split(t.slides[1]['ask'], dict(counts=[22, 1, 1, 0], n=24))
assert not is_split(t.slides[2]['ask'], dict(counts=[0, 0, 0], n=0))
assert share_right(dict(kind='order', options=['a', 'b', 'c'], answer=[2, 0, 1]), dict(counts=[3, 1], n=4)) == .75
assert share_right(dict(kind='words', q='Q?', most=80), dict(n=9)) is None and not is_split(dict(kind='words', q='Q?', most=80), dict(n=9))

The recap data: the ideas to follow up, the primers beside a slide, and the questions. The room is not the owner, so the run adds no attempt.

rc = recap(t, r)
assert rc.follow == ['sequential-computation', 'scaling-by-the-root-of-dk'] and rc.beside == [dict(slug='softmax', slide='s3', at=420., secs=120., ask=None, main=None)]
assert rc.questions[0]['text'] == 'Is √dk the best number?' and len(lr.attempts(limit=1000)) == 0   # the room is not the owner
assert [(x['slide'], x['secs'], x['share']) for x in rc.slides] == [('s1', 60., None), ('s2', 240., 22/24), ('s3', 900., .4)]

A question on the idea of a primer goes into its beside entry. When most hands chose a wrong option, weak and recap show it after its slide, and the follow-up walk has its idea.

r2 = new_run(t, now=0.)
qa = dict(kind='choice', q='What does softmax give?', options=['Weights that add to 1', 'The largest score'], answer=0)
log_beside(r2, 'softmax', 's3', at=10., secs=60., ask=qa, main=1)
assert r2['beside'] == [dict(slug='softmax', slide='s3', at=10., secs=60., ask=qa, main=1)] and r2['beside'][0]['ask'] is not qa   # a copy
w = weak(t, r2, names={'softmax': 'Softmax'})
assert w == [dict(slide='s3', title='Softmax (beside idea 3)', beside='softmax', share=None, top_wrong='The largest score', n=None, main=1)]
assert recap(t, r2).follow == ['softmax'] and recap(t, r2).unsure[0]['title'] == 'softmax (beside idea 3)'   # no names: the slug
log_beside(r2, 'softmax', 's3', at=80., secs=5., ask=qa, rounds=[dict(counts=[9, 1], n=10)])
assert len(weak(t, r2)) == 1 and r2['beside'][1]['rounds'] == [dict(counts=[9, 1], n=10)]   # 90% right is not weak

The recap file has no script and no notes. It has the figures inline, the right answers and the shares, and the text from the room is escaped.

log_question(r, '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>', at=440., shown=True)
page = recap_html(t, r, asset_resolver(lr))
assert '<script' not in page.lower() and 'src="http' not in page and 'Softmax makes weights' not in page
assert 'data:image/png;base64,' in page and '✓ Right' in page and '40% right' in page and 'It keeps the variance near 1.' in page
assert '<img src=x' not in page and '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>' in page

The file shows the hands, both rounds, and only the questions that the presenter kept.

log_question(r, 'A question that the presenter did not keep', at=450.)
page = recap_html(t, r, asset_resolver(lr))
assert 'Most hands: B (right: A)' in page and 'Round 1: 83% right' in page and 'Round 2: 92% right' in page
assert 'did not keep' not in page and page.count('✓ Right') == 3 and '"answer"' not in page

A bad right answer (below 0) gives no hands line, so no letter comes from the end of the list.

a = dict(kind='choice', q='Q?', options=['a', 'b'], answer=-1)
assert 'Most hands' not in _ask_html(a, dict(main=0)) and 'Most hands: A (right: B)' in _ask_html(a | dict(answer=1), dict(main=0))

A primer that was open beside a shown slide adds its question and its result under that slide. A primer with no question adds nothing.

r3 = deepcopy(r)
log_beside(r3, 'softmax', 's3', at=430., secs=30., ask=qa, main=1)
page = recap_html(t, r3, asset_resolver(lr))
sec = first(x for x in page.split('<section>') if x.startswith('<h2>' + html.escape(t.slides[2]['title'])))
assert 'What does softmax give?' in sec and 'Weights that add to 1' in sec and 'Most hands: B (right: A)' in sec
assert page.count('<p class="q">') == recap_html(t, r, asset_resolver(lr)).count('<p class="q">') + 1   # the entry with no question adds nothing

title: talk
section: Paper titles in walks and talks
text:
Paper titles in walks and talks
A PDF from arXiv can come in with its id, such as 1706.03762, as its title. The walk gets the title of the paper later (repair_paper_titles), but its steps, its talks, the sources of their slides and the sources of its concepts kept the id. repair_id_titles gives each of these the title of the paper, from the walk that reads it. The order of the lists stays, because a repair is not a change that you made.


source

Learning.repair_id_titles
def repair_id_titles()->list:
Give each title that is only an arXiv id, in a walk, a talk and the sources of a concept, the title of the paper from the walk that reads it. The order of the lists stays. Return the ids that changed.


A walk on the paper 1706.03762 has its real title, but its step, its talk and the source of its concept keep the id. The repair gives each the title of the paper. The talk does not say that its walk changed, and a second repair changes nothing.

lp = temp_learning()
lp.put('Attention', 'Weights from query-key dot products.', 'ml', provenance=[dict(src='vault', shelf='store', doc_id='d1', title='1706.03762')])
read = dict(src='vault:store', shelf='store', doc_id='d1', ref='d1', title='1706.03762', text='Attention maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output.')
lp.put_journey(dict(id='p1', title='Attention Is All You Need', mode='walk', steps=[dict(slug='attention', status='todo', check=dict(way='words', kind='short', depth=2), read=read)],
                    source=dict(shelf='store', doc_id='d1', url='https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762', title='Attention Is All You Need')))
tp = talk_from_walk(lp, Fake({}), 'p1', choice=False, fill=False)
lp.put_talk({**tp, 'title': '1706.03762'})
test_eq(sorted(lp.repair_id_titles()), sorted(['p1', tp.id, 'attention']))
test_eq(lp.concept('attention').provenance[0]['title'], 'Attention Is All You Need')
tp = lp.talk(tp.id)
test_eq((tp.title, tp.slides[0]['show']['src']['title'], lp.journey('p1').steps[0]['read']['title']), ('Attention Is All You Need',) * 3)
test_eq((walk_changes(lp, tp).changed, lp.repair_id_titles()), (0, []))   # a new title is not a change of the walk

title: llm
text:
This module connects the tutor to a model. The tutor needs only one function, ask(prompt, sp), which returns text. The module also parses JSON replies and gives Fake, a model for tests that runs offline.
Import the tools that this module uses.

title: llm
text:
The model
Each surface gives its own ask.



surface
ask




web app
route_ask: each call goes through the routing of ramabana, on a backend that stays open


notebook
rishi_ask: a new Chat of the model layer for each call


the ramabana terminal agent
agent.oneshot, so the routing of the agent applies


tests
Fake



The default model is --model, else $ABHYASA_MODEL, else DFLT_MODEL (claude/sonnet).


source

rishi_ask
def rishi_ask(
    model:str=None
):
An ask(prompt, sp='') on a new rishi.Chat (the model layer) for each call, on dflt_model(model).




source

dflt_model
def dflt_model(
    model:str=None
)->str:
model, else $ABHYASA_MODEL, else the setting models.default, else DFLT_MODEL.

title: llm
text:
JSON replies
parse_json finds the JSON in a reply. ask_json asks again one time when the reply is not valid JSON.


source

ask_json
def ask_json(
    ask, prompt:str, sp:str='', tries:int=2, need:tuple=()
):
Ask for JSON and parse it. On a bad reply, or one with no text in a key of need, ask one more time with the error.




source

parse_json
def parse_json(
    s:str
):
The first JSON object or array in s, also inside a ``fence. RaiseValueError` when there is none.


parse_json reads JSON in a fence, JSON inside other text, and arrays. A fence inside a JSON string does not break it. It fails when there is no JSON.

test_eq(parse_json('```json\n{"a": 1}\n```'), {'a': 1})
test_eq(parse_json('Here it is: {"a": [1, 2]} thanks'), {'a': [1, 2]})
test_eq(parse_json('[{"x": 1}]'), [{'x': 1}])
test_fail(lambda: parse_json('nothing'), contains='no JSON')
test_eq(parse_json('{"answer": "Use ```python\\nx = 1\\n``` here."}'), {'answer': 'Use ```python\nx = 1\n``` here.'})
test_eq(parse_json('Sure. {"a": 1} and then {"b": 2}'), {'a': 1})

title: llm
text:
A model for tests
Fake replies from a dict of rules. The first rule with a key in the prompt gives the reply. It sends a dict or a list reply as JSON. It keeps each call in calls.


source

Fake
def Fake(
    rules:dict=None, dflt:str='{}'
):
A stand-in model for tests: Fake({'grade': {...}, 'question': {...}}).


A matching rule gives its reply, and Fake records the call.

f = Fake({'GRADE': dict(correct=True)})
test_eq(ask_json(f, 'GRADE this'), dict(correct=True))
test_eq(len(f.calls), 1)

After a reply that is not JSON, ask_json asks again and gets the JSON.

bad = Fake(dict(X=lambda p, sp: 'oops' if 'not valid' not in p else '{"ok": 1}'))
test_eq(ask_json(bad, 'X'), {'ok': 1})

With need, a reply must be one JSON object with text in each of those keys. A list, or an object with no question, gets one more try. A second bad reply raises a ValueError that names the key.

odd = Fake(dict(Q=lambda p, sp: '{"question": "What is a rank?"}' if 'must be one JSON object' in p else '[1, 2]'))
test_eq(ask_json(odd, 'Q', need=('question',)), {'question': 'What is a rank?'})
test_fail(lambda: ask_json(Fake(dflt={}), 'Q', need=('question',)), contains='question')

title: llm
text:
A model for each task
The tutor does five tasks, and each task can use its own model. A quick model can grade and give hints. A strong model can write questions and lessons. The Settings page saves the choice. Router reads it on each call, so a change has an effect on the next call.



task
what the model does




question
writes a question and its hidden model answer


grade
reads the conversation and grades it


hint
gives the next hint


lesson
teaches the smallest step after a miss


extract
finds the concepts in a text



Each task also has a reply cap: the most tokens that the model can write in one reply. TOKENS gives the default of each task. A question has options and a rubric, and an extract can name 15 concepts, so these two get the most. A hint is short. The Settings page can change each cap. Only the cap is a setting, because ramabana’s oneshot uses no other per-call value: it turns thinking off, and the time limit of a model is in ramabana’s config.toml. The model layer gives the cap to the API models (OpenAI, Codex, Gemini, Copilot) and to the models on this Mac. Claude Code does not use it for the reply, but ramabana uses it to fit the prompt in the window of the model.
model_ask gives an ask for any model name. Install the models extra (pip install abhyasa[models]) to use the full list of models. With the extra, the name can be any model in that list: Claude Code, Codex, OpenAI, Copilot, Gemini, or a model on this machine (LiteRT, mlx, llama.cpp, Ollama). The call goes through the routing of ramabana, as route_ask below shows. Without the extra, the name goes to the model layer as it is.


source

model_ask
def model_ask(
